How about we keep the electoral college, but have it divided to counties, and not to states, and have the electors be the elected representatives of your county? The counties are each given votes based on population, but the elected officials must vote 50%+1 in favor of a candidate to have their county votes count.

This way the electoral college is more responsive at the local level, but is not as one-sided as the popular vote, it is forced to pick a popular candidate, and people will vote more often in midterm elections because their county reps will be held responsible for their presidential vote.

Furthermore we should have run-off elections, not this bullshit system that gravitates to a two party system.

I pushed this idea earlier in a discussion about the amendment proposed by California Senators. Essentially this seems like a good way to give the country local control without going to mob rule.

@Antikaon mentioned this point that I didn't consider:

Interesting idea. There is one overlooked factor though.

The legislative branch is split into two bodies for a reason. The Senate provides equal representation for each state. The House of Representatives provides equal representation for the people. In our check & balances system, the biggest check against the legislature is the executive branch, with the president wielding most of it's power.

With the electoral college, each state gets electors equal to the number of representatives plus the number of senators for that state. Therefore each state gets an equal say in the election and the people of the nation also get an equal say. This in combination with the "winner take all" system adopted by most states creates a process that mirrors the legislature as a whole and provides balance between the two branches of government. I think that's pretty important, and most people don't think about that part of it.

I think it would be good to force the electors to vote as directed though. The need for their autonomy passed long ago.

Theoretically I'd say each state would still have the same ratio of electors versus other states, but there would be more votes counted at the electoral college level, so its the same system with more local control.

"My father worked at the Ford engine assembly plant for 30 years and my brother for two while he saved money for college. There was an inverse relationship between the ascendency of the United Auto Workers union and the quality of US automobiles. When my father started at Ford in the early ’50s, the balance of power between Ford management and the UAW favored management. As the US became richer and more cars sold, Ford’s goal transitioned from producing quality cars at a profit to producing a profit for the least investment. Along with this, the UAW’s goal changed from protecting its members to enriching and protecting itself. Union feather-bedding grew to nearly unsustainable proportions, both in union management and on the factory floor. Union management was populated by people who’d never set foot on a factory floor, while nearly illiterate line workers filled the ranks of the hourly workers, workers with an entitlement attitude. My father, who worked in maintenance, told stories of equipment going offline because of parts pilferage and workers finding out-of-the-way places to drink, gamble, or sleep. My brother’s job was to break down engines that were inoperative and send the parts back through the assembly line; about one in five from his experience in the ’70s. He told stories of missing valves, pistons installed incorrectly, and hamburger wrappers and other trash found inside cylinders. All the while, wages and benefits skyrocketed as the UAW became de facto management. He told stories of engines with missing parts because female line workers were put into positions where they did not have the strength to install parts, so they just didn’t. Incompetent employees were unfire-able, instead reassigned to less-and-less demanding positions. Lay-offs were obsolete. Unneeded employees were put in “employee banks” where they were supposed to show up for “work” and sit in employee lounges on the off chance they might be again be needed. Guess how many actually showed up. Those actually laid off were paid 75-percent of their base pay not to work."
